package_info.package_manager: custom/unknown (malware distributed as Windows binaries, not via public package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (multiple versions and modules, not versioned as a package)
package_info.why_malicious: ModPipe is a modular backdoor malware specifically designed to target Oracle Micros RES 3700 PoS systems. It enables attackers to exfiltrate sensitive data, including credentials, process information, and system configuration, and provides remote control and persistence on infected systems. Its modular architecture allows for dynamic loading of additional malicious capabilities, making it highly adaptable and stealthy.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Initial dropper containing both 32-bit and 64-bit binaries, installs persistent loader.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At initial infection, the dropper writes both 32-bit and 64-bit loader binaries to disk, configures persistence by modifying system startup settings, and enables subsequent stages of the malware to execute automatically.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Droppers that install persistent loaders and deploy multiple architecture binaries are typical of malware aiming for broad compatibility and stealthy persistence.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software installers do not silently install persistent loaders or drop multiple architecture binaries without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise installers may deploy both 32/64-bit binaries, but not with hidden persistent loaders or without user notification.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Persistent loader unpacks and loads the next stage of the malware into memory.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At system startup, the loader unpacks the main module from encrypted storage, injects it into a target process's memory space, and initiates the main backdoor functionality.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unpacking and injecting code into other processes is a hallmark of malware seeking to evade detection and maintain persistence.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate loaders do not inject arbitrary code into unrelated processes or unpack encrypted payloads at startup.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some security or update tools may unpack code, but do not inject into unrelated processes or use encrypted payloads without clear justification.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Main module implements command-and-control (C&C) communication, module management, and data exfiltration.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the main module establishes outbound connections to hardcoded C&C servers, receives and processes remote commands, dynamically loads additional modules, and exfiltrates collected data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: C&C communication, remote command execution, and modular architecture are classic backdoor behaviors that enable attackers to control infected systems and expand capabilities.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not connect to untrusted remote servers for command execution or download and execute arbitrary modules from external sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise management tools may use remote commands, but only with strong authentication and trusted infrastructure.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: GetMicInfo module extracts MICROS POS database usernames and passwords.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When triggered by the C&C, the GetMicInfo module accesses MICROS POS configuration files or process memory, extracts database credentials, and prepares this sensitive information for exfiltration to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Extracting credentials from POS systems is a direct violation of system security and privacy, enabling further compromise and data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate modules do not extract or exfiltrate sensitive credentials without explicit user authorization and secure handling.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or migration tools may access credentials, but only with user consent and secure storage.
key_indicators: Access to POS configuration files or memory

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: ModScan 2.20 module scans the local network and collects additional MICROS POS environment data.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When triggered, the ModScan module scans specified IP ranges on the local network for MICROS POS systems, collects environment and configuration data, and transmits the results to the C&C server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Network scanning and environment reconnaissance are typical prelude activities for lateral movement or further exploitation within a compromised environment.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate POS software does not perform unauthorized network scans or exfiltrate environment data to external servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Network management tools may scan networks, but only with administrative approval and for legitimate inventory purposes.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: ProcList module enumerates all running processes on the infected machine.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When triggered, the ProcList module enumerates all running processes on the infected system, compiles a list, and sends this information to the C&C server for attacker analysis.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Process enumeration is often used by malware to identify security software, high-value targets, or to plan further attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not exfiltrate process lists to external servers or perform enumeration without user knowledge.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System monitoring tools may enumerate processes, but do not transmit this data externally without consent.
key_indicators: Process enumeration of all running processes
Exfiltration of process list to C&C

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Main module command handler supports commands: 0x01 (Exit), 0x05 (Update C&C list), 0x0A/0x0B/0x0C (Insert/execute module), 0x0D (Transfer command to module), 0x0E (Uninstall module), 0x0F (Save network config).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the main module processes C&C commands to control malware behavior, including updating C&C addresses, loading and executing modules, transferring commands to modules, uninstalling modules, and saving network configuration, thereby enabling dynamic reconfiguration and control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote command processing and dynamic reconfiguration are core features of advanced persistent threats, allowing attackers to adapt malware behavior post-infection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not accept arbitrary remote commands to alter its behavior or configuration without secure authentication and user oversight.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote management tools may accept commands, but only with strong authentication and audit trails.
key_indicators: Remote command handler with multiple command types

attack_chain.action: Initial dropper is executed, installing persistent loader and next-stage binaries.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and loader execution at system startup

attack_chain.action: Persistent loader unpacks and injects the main module into a target process at startup.
attack_chain.leads_to: Main module execution and C&C communication

attack_chain.action: Main module establishes C&C communication, receives commands, and manages additional modules.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious modules and data exfiltration

attack_chain.action: Downloadable modules (GetMicInfo, ModScan, ProcList) are executed on demand to harvest credentials, scan the network, and enumerate processes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive data to C&C servers

behavioral_signatures: Installation of persistent loaders that unpack and inject code at startup
Unpacking of encrypted payloads and process injection into unrelated processes
Dynamic downloading and execution of additional modules on demand
Credential harvesting from POS configuration files or process memory
Network scanning for POS systems and environment reconnaissance
Enumeration and exfiltration of running process lists
file_indicators: Presence of unknown binaries with dropper or loader characteristics in system directories
Unusual files in startup locations (e.g., Windows registry Run keys, Startup folder) or scheduled tasks
Encrypted storage files used by malware for configuration (e.g., non-standard files with high entropy in application data folders)
network_indicators: Connections to C&C domains: subzeroday.zapto.org, shj145ertyb.ddns.net/gettime.html, ouidji12345.ddns.net/gettime.html
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the creation and execution of unknown binaries in startup locations, especially those that unpack or inject code into other processes. Detect outbound connections to known C&C IPs and domains. Look for unauthorized access to POS configuration files, credential harvesting, and network scanning activity. Correlate process enumeration and exfiltration events with suspicious network activity. Use endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools to flag process injection, dynamic module loading, and encrypted configuration storage behaviors.
